entries.title: Israel’s Eisenkot secures first coalition partner in bid to form government
entries.summary: The Yashar party says it agreed to sign a coalition pact with Israel's Our Home party, led by Avigdor Lieberman.
entries.content:
The Yashar party says it agreed to sign a coalition pact with Israel’s Our Home party, led by Avigdor Lieberman.

Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party has announced an agreement to unite with a right-wing opposition party in a bid to form the next Israeli government following October’s elections.

The Yashar party said on Tuesday that it agreed to sign a coalition pact with Israel’s Our Home party after a meeting with its leader Avigdor Lieberman, the first alliance of its kind since the election.

After no party managed to secure a 61-seat majority, Israel’s parliament was sworn in on November 10 without a new government.

President Isaac Herzog tasked Eisenkot with forming ⁠a government, while Benjamin Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister despite the October 27 election stripping Netanyahu of his majority.

Eisenkot has until December 6 to form a government under a 28-day mandate, though he could ask for a 14-day extension. If Eisenkot fails, Netanyahu would have an opportunity to do so. If no one is able to form a government, another election will be held next year.

Arab parties

The agreement between Eisenkot, whose party won 21 parliament seats, and Lieberman, whose party won seven, was unforeseen since Lieberman has been vocal about his opposition to forming a government with support from Arab parties as well as to a unity government with Netanyahu.

Lieberman had once served as foreign minister under a previous Netanyahu government but has since become a strong critic.

Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud’s alliance with far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties outperformed election expectations but still lost its majority. It now holds 53 of the Knesset’s 120 seats.

Eisenkot’s centre-right Yashar party and patchwork coalition partners, including Lieberman, hold just 48 seats. But they have potential allies in the parties representing Israel’s Arab minority, which hold 19 seats and ⁠are aligned with Eisenkot in their vehement opposition to Netanyahu.

The path forward

Talks are also ongoing between Eisenkot, some of his “change bloc” partners and Likud on forming a unity government.

The left-wing Democrats party, which won eight parliament seats, separately said it was suspending talks with Eisenkot after the Yashar party leader’s talks with Netanyahu’s Likud on a possible unity government.

Yair Golan, head of the Democrats, said he prefers a government without Netanyahu but with Arab parties.

entries.title: Poll finds US voters want government to end Iran war regardless of terms
entries.summary: New survey finds that 55 percent of voters, including 80 percent of Democrats, want war brought to an end immediately.
entries.content:
New survey finds that 55 percent of voters, including 80 percent of Democrats, want the Iran war brought to an end immediately.

A new poll has found that a majority of voters in the United States want an end to the US-Israel war on Iran immediately, even if it means accepting less favourable conditions.

Overall, 55 percent of those surveyed agreed with an “end to the war now, regardless of the terms”.

That number was even higher among Democrats and independents, who agreed with the statement at a rate of 80 percent and 59 percent, respectively. About 25 percent of Republicans said the same.

A majority of Democratic voters also supported steps to pressure the administration of President Donald Trump to stop the conflict.

Fifty-three percent of party members said they would favour Congress withholding funding for military operations, and 51 percent would back an “an Iran war-funding cutoff” in upcoming budget negotiations, even if the manoeuvre risked a government shutdown.

The numbers were published on Tuesday as part of the latest Critical Issues Poll, released by the University of Maryland and the research firm Ipsos.

Shibley Telhami, the poll’s principal investigator, said he was surprised by the level of support for ending the war, regardless of the terms.

“We knew that people were strongly opposed to this war and wanted it to end,” he told Al Jazeera in a phone call. “What we were less sure of is what they would be willing to accept to achieve this.”

The survey asked 1,022 US adults about their perspectives on the war.

In one question, they were tasked with assessing with three options: whether to end the conflict immediately, escalate militarily, or continue on the current path in order to extract concessions from Iran.

Just 21 percent of all respondents favoured the current path, and 18 percent supported escalation.

“Clearly, the public mood is to end it now, whatever it takes,” said Telhami.

Questioning the rationale for war

Voters also appear sceptical about the US government’s arguments in favour of the war, which include dismantling Iran’s nuclear programme.

The Critical Issues Poll found that only 28 percent of those surveyed believed that the war had left Iran in “worse position” to develop nuclear weapons.

While the US has long voiced concerned that Iran could pursue nuclear arms, intelligence assessments have not found evidence that Tehran has authorised such a step since abandoning its nuclear weapons programme in 2003.

The Strait of Hormuz has also emerged as a key issue, with Iran closing the waterway to commercial traffic early in the war. The Trump administration has responded with a naval blockade in the strait.

Some 20 percent of the world’s oil supply passes through the maritime artery, and fuel prices have spiked as a result of the war.

About 35 percent of respondents in Tuesday’s poll said that they believe Iran is now in control of the strait, while just 12.7 percent said the US is in control.

The poll comes as the Democratic Party is debating how far it should go to end the unpopular war.

In the recent midterm elections, backlash against the war — and as well as related issues like rising fuel prices — contributed to big gains for the Democratic Party.

Trump’s Republican Party, meanwhile, suffered one of its most bruising setbacks in modern US history, losing control of both chambers of Congress.

Members of the Democratic Party’s anti-war left have pointed to the results as proof that voters want an end to the war and an end to US support for Israel.

But that position has brought them into conflict with members of the party’s more hawkish establishment wing.

While leaders such as Representative Hakeem Jeffries and Senator Chuck Schumer have both expressed support for ending the war, they have yet to commit to aggressive strategies to reach that goal.

That includes potentially cutting off funding for military operations against Iran, or using an upcoming funding battle in December to demand that the White House end the war.

“A lot of Democratic figures are dismissing the intensity of public feeling on this issue,” said Telhami. “If they don’t adapt, they will be left behind.”

He added that progressive figures such as Senator Bernie Sanders and Senator Chris Van Hollen have been among those pressing for a more assertive stance.

Van Hollen, who is challenging Schumer to lead the Democratic majority in the US Senate, has used the war to portray the party’s moderate leadership as out of step with voters.

The poll found that Democratic voters prefer Van Hollen over Schumer by a ratio of nearly three to one.

entries.title: Alaska ends deal to give voter records to US Justice Department
entries.summary: The decision follows the conclusion of the 2026 midterm elections and an effort under Trump to gather state voter rolls.
entries.content:
The decision follows the conclusion of the 2026 midterm elections and an effort under Trump to collect state voter rolls.

Alaska has terminated a memorandum of understanding that granted the United States Department of Justice (DOJ) access to the state’s voter rolls.

On Monday, outgoing Lieutenant Governor Nancy Dahlstrom, who oversees the state’s elections, announced she had notified the Justice Department that Alaska was withdrawing from the 2025 memo, effective immediately.

In a statement, Dahlstrom said her state had entered the agreement “in good faith to cooperate with our federal law enforcement partners”. But she acknowledged a shift had taken place after the 2026 midterm elections.

“The circumstances have now changed,” Dahlstrom wrote. “The election has concluded and the agreement no longer serves a continuing purpose.”

The reversal comes after months of pressure from the administration of President Donald Trump for states to surrender their voter rolls to federal authorities.

Trump has argued that such information was necessary to root out fraud during the November 3 midterms.

But officials in certain states argued that the federal government was encroaching on their constitutional authority. Under the US Constitution, only states have the power to administer elections.

Experts have also called Trump’s claims of “rigged” elections unsubstantiated.

No voters flagged for removal

The memorandum, signed last December at the Justice Department’s behest, established terms under which federal officials could flag potentially ineligible voters on Alaska’s voter rolls.

“Since that time, the DOJ has not identiﬁed any potentially ineligible voters or raised concerns regarding Alaska’s voter registration records,” the state Division of Elections said.

“No voters were removed from Alaska’s voter rolls as a result of the agreement.”

The announcement came as the state certified its November 3 midterm election results, in which Democrats flipped a Senate seat and won the governor’s office.

Alaska was one of several surprise battlegrounds during the midterms.

Democrat Mary Peltola unseated two-term Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in a fiercely contested Senate race marred by allegations of a spoiler candidate recruited to sabotage the senator’s re-election bid.

Meanwhile, Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins won the state’s governorship, ending nearly three decades of Republican control in that office.

Democrats nationwide made significant gains, flipping both chambers of Congress in the midterms.

That result was largely fuelled by voter frustration under Trump, whose Republican Party suffered defeats in former strongholds like Texas.

A legal battle over voter rolls

Faced with drooping approval ratings in the lead-up to the election, Trump had falsely claimed that many non-citizens were registered to vote across the country.

His administration sued some 30 states as well as Washington, DC, after they declined to hand over their unredacted voter rolls for review.

Twenty-eight of those cases were ultimately dismissed in court, according to the Brennan Center for Justice, a public policy institute at New York University.

The Justice Department suffered a further setback last month when a federal judge struck down its nationwide voter-list maintenance programme, ruling that it lacked legal authority to collect and assess state registration lists. The administration has appealed the ruling.

Alaska was one of at least 16 states that complied with the administration’s demands for voter roll access.

But it was sued by voting rights advocates for surrendering voter information, in violation of the Alaska Constitution.

In its Monday statement, Alaska’s Division of Elections said it had directed the Justice Department to destroy Alaska’s confidential voter information in accordance with the 2025 memo — a move that could have implications for the pending lawsuit.

On Tuesday, Democratic State Senator Bill Wielechowski suggested the latest termination was timed to prevent further scrutiny from the lawsuit.

“The real reason they did this is to try to make the lawsuit over this release go away before the incoming Gov. Kreiss-Tomkins Administration could settle or produce discovery,” Wielechowski wrote on social media.

Kreiss-Tomkins is set to be sworn in as governor on December 7.

Wielechowski also noted that Alaska’s request for the Trump administration to delete the records is “likely meaningless”, since federal authorities have “undoubtedly already loaded it” onto government databases.

In its Monday statement, Alaska’s Division of Elections said its decision to end the memo did not constitute an admission of wrongdoing.

The state’s interests, it added, were “best served by terminating the agreement and continuing to rely on its established voter list-maintenance procedures”.

A Justice Department spokesperson told The Associated Press on Tuesday that the department would issue a formal response to the state.

entries.title: Rebel group retreats in DR Congo after heavy clashes with government forces
entries.summary: CRP halts advance towards Bunia, citing commitments made during Ugandan-mediated talks with government.
entries.content:
CRP halts advance towards Bunia, citing commitments made during Ugandan-mediated talks with the government.

The rebel group led by convicted war criminal Thomas Lubanga has withdrawn from areas recently seized in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) after days of heavy fighting with government forces.

The Convention for the Popular Revolution (CRP) announced on Tuesday that it had decided to halt an advance towards the town of Bunia, the capital of Ituri province in northeast DRC.

In a statement, the group cited a commitment made in talks with the Congolese government, mediated by Uganda’s President Yoweri Museveni, as one of the reasons for its withdrawal.

The CRP’s decision came one day after the group seized the Iga-Barriere, a strategic area about 25km north of Bunia, forcing government troops to withdraw towards the provincial capital.

Lubanga, a former leader of the Union of Congolese Patriots, was convicted by the International Criminal Court (ICC) in 2012 on charges of recruiting and using child soldiers.

He was sentenced to 14 years in prison and released in March 2020 after completing his sentence. Lubanga remains sanctioned by the United Nations.

Lubanga announced the formation of the CRP in 2025, opening another front against the DRC’s President Felix Tshisekedi.

The group said the decision to withdraw troops was made “out of respect for the commitments made at the State House” by the Congolese government and the CRP, referring to an October 9 meeting hosted by Uganda between Lubanga and a delegation of senior government and military officials.

Disrupting Ebola response

On Sunday, the World ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌Health Organization said fighting near a hospital in the Ituri ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠province, north of Bunia, forced the evacuation of health workers and aid partners, disrupting Ebola response efforts.

The DRC is experiencing its largest and deadliest Ebola outbreak, which has spread across the country’s east and northeast. Ituri remains one of the most affected provinces.

Thousands of civilians have reportedly been displaced towards Bunia since the weekend due to renewed fighting between rebel fighters and government forces, according to local media reports.

entries.title: South Africa convicts Zimbabwean who tried to fight Ukraine for Russia
entries.summary: The Zimbabwean man was arrested on November 8 at a Johannesburg airport while attempting to board a flight to Russia.
entries.content:
The Zimbabwean man was arrested on November 8 at a Johannesburg airport while attempting to board a flight to Russia.

A South African court has convicted and sentenced a Zimbabwean man for trying to travel to Russia to fight in Ukraine after he was arrested earlier this month alongside eight others.

Tafadzwa Sithole was sentenced to five years in prison on Tuesday, under a five-year suspension, meaning he would only have to serve the time if he is convicted of a similar crime within that time period. Sithole is set to be deported back to Zimbabwe.

He told the court that he had agreed to fight for Russia in the war in exchange for “remuneration” after successfully applying online in Zimbabwe.

“He knew that the Russian Federation was engaged in an ongoing armed conflict with Ukraine and that the military service he intended to render would be performed in the context of that armed conflict,” his lawyer told the court.

Sithole was arrested at OR Tambo international airport on November 8 while attempting to board a flight to Russia.

Foreign Military Assistance Act

Sithole said a person he identified as “Albina” contacted him after he submitted the application, arranged accommodation in South Africa and provided a flight ticket to Russia. His admissions were detailed in a plea agreement with South African prosecutors.

He pleaded guilty to violating the Regulation of Foreign Military Assistance Act. The act prohibits mercenary activity and regulates military assistance to parties in foreign conflicts, including recruitment and training, and also applies to foreign nationals.

Sithole, who described himself as an unemployed third-year student at a university in Zimbabwe, appeared in court with four other accused who are also negotiating plea agreements with prosecutors.

He said he entered South Africa legally on November 4 and stayed in an accommodation in Kempton Park, east of Johannesburg, in preparation for his travel to Russia.

Larger issue at play

Zimbabwe is among several African countries where Russia has been recruiting fighters for its war against Ukraine. Others include South Africa, Kenya, Botswana and Ghana.

Zimbabwean authorities said in March that 15 citizens had been killed in the war in Ukraine and that they were seeking the return of 66 others. The government said recruits were promised well-paid jobs but had their travel documents confiscated and were forced into combat.

Kenya’s government said in February that more than 1,000 citizens had been recruited to fight for Russia. Families protested in Nairobi in March, demanding their relatives’ return and the prosecution of those responsible.

An investigation by Code for Africa, a nonprofit data journalism and technology organisation, identified 289 websites, domains and social media profiles used to lure recruits through false advertising and promises of generous benefits.

entries.title: Arsenal and Dortmund draw 1-1 as Gyokeres goes from hero to villain
entries.summary: Arsenal dominate the chances as Borussia Dortmund fight back for a 1-1 draw in football's Champions League.
entries.content:
Arsenal dominate the chances as Borussia Dortmund fight back for a 1-1 draw in football’s Champions League.

Arsenal striker Viktor Gyokeres showed why he is such a polarising figure with a thunderous goal and a crucial miss in Tuesday’s 1-1 draw against Borussia Dortmund in the Champions League.

Gunners boss Mikel Arteta had urged Gyokeres to seize his opportunity after selecting the Swedish striker instead of Kai Havertz for the league phase tie at London’s Emirates Stadium.

Initially, Gyokeres looked like he was doing just that with his first goal at Emirates this season, and only his third for the Gunners in all competitions.

But the 28-year-old has been much maligned for his erratic displays since arriving from Sporting Lisbon in 2025.

And he gave more ammunition to his critics when he missed a golden opportunity to seal the points with a woeful header in the closing stages.

Dortmund had equalised through Maximilian Beier by then, and Arteta was left to rue his decision to put his faith in Gyokeres.

Arsenal are unbeaten in their last 11 games in all competitions, but this was not a vintage display by the English champions, who failed to win at home for the first time this season.

In a showdown between the current leaders of the Premier League and the Bundesliga, Arsenal were too profligate in attack and error-prone at the back to say they deserved all three points.

Arsenal sit fifth in the league phase with three wins and two draws from their five matches, while seventh-placed Dortmund are one point behind them.

Arteta will hope for a much more ruthless display in a significant Premier League showdown with spluttering title rivals Manchester City in north London on Sunday.

Arsenal were in control at the start, and Christos Tzolis’s strike bounced just over before Gyokeres tested Dortmund keeper Gregor Kobel with a long-range drive.

It was a warning Dortmund failed to heed as Gyokeres put Arsenal ahead in the 10th minute.

Fatally backing off when Gyokeres took possession 25 yards from goal, Dortmund’s defenders were punished by the Swede as he unleashed a superb dipping strike that flashed into the roof of the net.

Arsenal’s luck runs out in Champions League

Tzolis nearly doubled Arsenal’s lead with a curler that forced a sprawling save from Kobel.

Declan Rice almost replicated Gyokeres’s goal with a ferocious blast that fizzed just over.

Kepa Arrizabalaga was deputising for David Raya in goal for Arsenal after his fellow Spaniard suffered a shoulder injury in Saturday’s draw at Newcastle.

Such was Arsenal’s dominance that Kepa did not make a save until the final minute of the first half when he blocked Joane Gadou’s shot at the near post.

But Dortmund have a well-earned reputation as a stronger team in the second half this season, and they lived up to that tag once again.

Dortmund had a strong penalty appeal rejected after Gyokeres blocked a corner with his arm.

And with Arsenal unusually sloppy at the back, Dortmund’s pressure was rewarded in the 55th minute.

Gadou surged towards the Arsenal area before slipping a pass into Beier, who eluded Gabriel Magalhaes to plant a clinical low finish past Kepa.

Kobel saved Piero Hincapie’s close-range header as Arsenal tried to respond, while Dortmund midfielder Jobe Bellingham had a goal disallowed for a tight offside.

Gyokeres wasted his chance to finish as Arsenal’s hero for once when he sent a close-range diving header woefully wide from Martin Odegaard’s cross.

Arsenal’s luck was out after Odegaard’s delivery twice hit the post and appeared to strike Serhou Guirassy’s hand before it was finally scrambled clear.

Rice was equally unfortunate with a first-time drive that cannoned back off the near post to leave Arsenal frustrated.
